name: known_divergences_catalog
description: Machine-readable catalog of ACCEPTED cross-SDK divergences - the allowlist the parity discipline checks against. Every entry must carry exactly the keys id, sdk, category, status, description, parity_scope, allowed_difference, tracking; status has exactly one legal value, 'intended' - a divergence that is not intended is a bug to fix, never a row to add. `sdk` names the SDK whose behavior differs from the shared contract ('ts' or 'py'). `parity_scope` states what MUST remain identical despite the divergence; `allowed_difference` states precisely what is permitted to differ - an entry whose allowed_difference would cover an enforcement-verdict difference is invalid by policy, not just by schema. Structure is validated by BOTH test suites (sdk-typescript/tests/unit/fixture-bookkeeping.test.ts, sdk-python/tests/test_fixture_bookkeeping.py), so a malformed or vocabulary-expanding entry fails CI in either language. The narrative History of fixed divergences stays in known-divergences.md - this catalog replaces only the live table.

categories.enforcement_surface: one SDK applies an identical verdict through a weaker or different mechanism
categories.evaluation_context: one SDK evaluates a rule with less context on some path
categories.dependency: a capability resolves through an optional dependency in one SDK
categories.capability: a control or emission exists in only one SDK today

entries.description: Signed-policy verification backend: TypeScript verifies Ed25519 with node:crypto, always present. Python has no stdlib Ed25519, so policy_verify.py resolves an OPTIONAL backend (cryptography, then PyNaCl). With policy_public_key pinned and neither installed, Python reaches a state TypeScript cannot: it cannot check the signature at all. The package ships zero mandatory runtime dependencies, and the degraded state is declared rather than hidden.
entries.parity_scope: All shared signature vectors resolve to identical verdicts once a backend is installed (pip install "obsvr-sdk[crypto]", included in the dev extra so CI runs them for real); Python still fails closed without one - the fetched policy is refused, last-good stays in force, and policy_verification_unavailable is stamped into reserved metadata on every subsequent event.
entries.allowed_difference: The unverifiable-but-declared degraded state exists only in Python, only with a pinned key and no optional crypto backend.
entries.tracking: sdk-python/obsvr/policy_verify.py. The two vectors this reaches are marked sdk_support py:optional in fixtures/policy_signature.json - valid_signature_accepts and forged_value_reject, the only two that need real Ed25519 arithmetic rather than a structural refusal - so the corpus points here and this points back. Closes if a stdlib Ed25519 ever lands or the dependency posture changes.

entries.description: Per-call network attribution: TypeScript accepts client_ip and user_agent on the call, extracts them off the provider arguments and writes them onto the audit event (proxy/filters/filter.ts, proxy/types.ts). Python has NO capture path for either - no per-call keyword argument, no config default - so events.py emits a hardcoded None for both. Its per-call channel is a namespaced keyword argument carrying identity keys, and these two are not among them.
entries.parity_scope: The audit event SCHEMA is identical: both SDKs emit client_ip and user_agent fields on every event, and both strip these keys from the outbound provider request so following the published type cannot break a call. Every other attribution field - user_id, service_name, tenant, session - is captured on both sides, though the channels that ESTABLISH those values differ by SDK: TypeScript accepts typed per-call audit fields on the provider call, Python's per-call channel is the namespaced obsvr_metadata keyword argument, and both resolve wrap-time options and the ambient use_subject()/useSubject() scope (see KD-11 for the one evaluation-context edge). Nothing about a policy verdict differs; the same rules over the same input yield the same action_taken in both SDKs whether or not these two fields carry a value.
entries.allowed_difference: Python records null for client_ip and user_agent where TypeScript can record a caller-supplied value. A consumer correlating events by client IP or user agent gets those fields only from TypeScript-emitted events.
entries.tracking: sdk-python/obsvr/events.py, where the two hardcoded Nones carry a comment saying so - a reader of a hardcoded empty value is entitled to know whether it is a default or a dead end. Closes when Python grows a per-call channel for the two network fields. Catalogued here rather than left in that comment alone because this list is read as the complete machine-readable inventory of accepted divergences, and a capability gap that appears only in a source comment is invisible to anyone trusting it. This is a CAPABILITY divergence and not a verdict one, so unlike the regex-dialect splits it is eligible for this catalog at all - those stay enumerated in SECURITY.md because an entry whose allowed_difference covers an enforcement-verdict difference is invalid by this catalog's own policy.

entries.description: Resolved-model provenance: when a provider answers with a model identifier different from the one the caller asked for, TypeScript records the served identifier in model_resolved and how it learned it in provenance_source, threading both through the client proxy, the shared integration event builder and nine integrations. Python's build_audit_event accepts neither parameter, so no Python surface can carry them and neither key appears anywhere in a Python-emitted event. Measured against one server returning a resolved identifier distinct from the requested one: TypeScript records it on every row, Python records null on every row.
entries.parity_scope: The model the CALLER requested is captured identically by both SDKs in the `model` field, on every surface, and is what every model_gate rule evaluates - so no policy verdict differs. Nothing about enforcement, signing, or the chain is affected: model_resolved is descriptive provenance about the response, not an input to any decision.
entries.allowed_difference: Python records no model_resolved and no provenance_source, so a consumer reconciling which model actually served a request - an alias resolving to a dated snapshot, or a quantised local build - can do so only from TypeScript-emitted events. Python's Vertex integration is the one partial exception: it smuggles a model_resolved value through the generic metadata map, with no provenance_source beside it.
entries.tracking: sdk-python/obsvr/events.py (build_audit_event has no parameter for either field) and sdk-python/obsvr/integrations/vertex.py (the metadata-map exception). Closes when the Python event builder grows both parameters and the surfaces thread them. Catalogued for the same reason as KD-9 and eligible on the same test: it is a CAPABILITY divergence, not a verdict one. It was carried until now as a prose row in an internal remediation inventory's still-open table, which is not the machine-readable catalog a reader trusting this file is consulting.

entries.description: Ambient-subject reach on the ENFORCING channel of the non-generic Python integrations: both SDKs establish a per-request principal ambently (use_subject() in Python, useSubject() in TypeScript), and in both the ambient subject reaches the signed event principal on every surface and both channels of the generic tool governor. TypeScript additionally resolves the ambient subject into the integration path's rules-evaluation identity (integrations/core.ts) and the wrap path's session-taint key (proxy/wrapper.ts). Python's non-generic integration surfaces (pydantic_ai, bedrock, vertex, haystack, mcp, autogen) build their rules-evaluation identity metadata from wrap-time options only, so an ambient subject present at call time is recorded on their signed events but does not key their user-scoped quota buckets or session-taint latch.
entries.parity_scope: An EXPLICIT identity (wrap-time user_id/service_name/metadata, or a per-call channel) resolves identically on every surface in both SDKs, and always wins over the ambient subject in both. The ambient subject fills the signed principal on every surface in both SDKs. On the generic tool governor (govern_tool / obsvrGovernTool) the ambient subject scopes signed and enforcing channels identically in both languages. The same rules over the same identity metadata yield the same verdict in both SDKs - what differs is which identity metadata reaches evaluation on the named surfaces when only an ambient subject is present.
entries.allowed_difference: On the named Python integration surfaces, a call whose only identity is the ambient subject evaluates user-scoped quota and session-taint against the wrap-time identity or the shared bucket, while the same call in TypeScript evaluates against the ambient subject. No explicit-identity call differs anywhere.
entries.tracking: The _identity_meta folds in sdk-python/obsvr/integrations/{pydantic_ai,bedrock,vertex,haystack,mcp,autogen}.py, against the ambient-consulting fold in sdk-python/obsvr/integrations/tools.py (_identity_meta) and sdk-typescript/src/integrations/core.ts. Closes when those folds consult obsvr.subject.get_current_subject() the way the tool governor's does; the tree scan test_every_pre_call_evaluation_threads_the_caller_identity already enumerates exactly the call sites to change.
